front_blocks.md: Define a **scalar** quantity.

back_blocks.md: A **scalar** is a quantity that has a **size (magnitude)** only, with no direction attached to it.
Distance, speed, time and mass are the scalars you meet in mechanics, and none of them can be negative.

front_blocks.md: Define a **vector** quantity.

back_blocks.md: A **vector** is a quantity that has a **direction** as well as a size (magnitude).
Displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, weight and momentum are all vectors, and their components can be positive or negative.

front_blocks.md: A ball rolls **forwards** 60 cm before stopping. Is that a scalar or a vector quantity, and why?

back_blocks.md: It is a **vector**.
The number 60 cm on its own would be a **distance**, which is a scalar. The word **forwards** attaches a direction to it, and a quantity with both a size and a direction is a vector.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Two objects with velocities of $7 \text{m s}^{-1}$ and $- 7 \text{m s}^{-1}$ are travelling at the same speed.

back_blocks.md: **True.**
Velocity is a **vector**, so the minus sign records only the **direction** of travel: the two objects are moving in opposite directions.
Speed is the scalar that goes with velocity, so it keeps the size and drops the direction, and both objects have a speed of $7 \text{m s}^{-1}$.

front_blocks.md: How are vector quantities distinguished from scalars in printed text, and how should you distinguish them in handwriting?

back_blocks.md: In print a vector is set in **bold**, non-italic type, as in $F$ or $a$.
You cannot write in bold, so in handwriting a vector is **underlined** instead.

front_blocks.md: Define **fundamental (S.I.) units**.

back_blocks.md: **Fundamental units**, or **S.I. units**, are the internationally standardised units used to measure the basic quantities.
The three needed in mechanics are the **metre** for length, the **second** for time and the **kilogram** for mass, and every other unit is built from them.

front_blocks.md: Convert 27.8 km and 3.8 hours into S.I. units.

back_blocks.md: Multiply each by the number of smaller units contained in one larger one:
There are 1000 metres in a kilometre, and $60 \times 60 = 3600$ seconds in an hour.

cards.front_md: Convert 27.8 km and 3.8 hours into S.I. units.
cards.back_md:
Multiply each by the number of smaller units contained in one larger one:

$27 . 8 \times 1000 = 27800 \text{m}$

$3 . 8 \times 3600 = 13680 \text{s}$

There are 1000 metres in a kilometre, and $60 \times 60 = 3600$ seconds in an hour.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
A time of 2 hours 30 minutes is 2.30 hours.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
There are 60 minutes in an hour rather than 100, so 30 minutes is **half** an hour and the time is **2.5 hours**.

front_blocks.md: Why must every quantity be converted into S.I. units before it is substituted into a mechanics formula?

back_blocks.md: The mechanics formulae relate **metres**, **seconds** and **kilograms** to one another, so they are only correct when every quantity is measured in those units.
Substituting a distance in kilometres alongside a time in seconds gives an answer that is in no consistent unit at all, and so means nothing.

front_blocks.md: Define a **derived unit**.

back_blocks.md: A **derived unit** is a unit made by combining the fundamental S.I. units of length, time and mass.
A density measured in $\text{kg m}^{-3}$ is one example, since it combines the kilogram with the metre.

front_blocks.md: Force $=$ mass $\times$ acceleration. What does that make the derived S.I. unit of force, and what is that unit normally called?

back_blocks.md: A mass in **kilograms** multiplied by an acceleration in $\text{m s}^{-2}$ gives a unit of $\text{kg m s}^{-2}$.
That combination is normally called the **newton**, written **N**, so $1 \text{N} = 1 \text{kg m s}^{-2}$.

front_blocks.md: An acceleration is measured in $\text{m s}^{-2}$. Fill in the blanks to read that unit back as a formula:

back_blocks.md: The completed formula is:
$\text{acceleration} = \frac{\text{velocity}}{\text{time}}$
$\text{m s}^{-2}$ is $\text{m s}^{-1}$ divided again by seconds, and $\text{m s}^{-1}$ is the unit of velocity. Reading a unit this way will give you back a formula you have forgotten.

back_blocks.md: Convert the kilometres and the hours separately, remembering that the hours are **squared**:

cards.back_md:

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Speed and velocity are measured in the same derived unit.

back_blocks.md: **True.**
A direction is not something a unit can record, so attaching one to a speed leaves the unit unchanged: both are measured in $\text{m s}^{-1}$.
What tells you which of the two you are looking at is the sign or the vector notation, never the unit.

front_blocks.md: Define a **force**.

back_blocks.md: A **force** is a push or a pull on an object.
It is a **vector**, so it has both a magnitude and a direction, and it is measured in **newtons (N)**.

front_blocks.md: Tension and thrust are both labelled $T$ N. What is the difference between them?

back_blocks.md: **Tension** is a **pulling** force, so it acts **away** from the object it is attached to, along the string or rod.
**Thrust**, also called compression, is a **pushing** force, so it acts **towards** the object.

front_blocks.md: Define the **weight** of an object.

back_blocks.md: An object's **weight** is the force on it produced by its mass and gravity, and it always acts **vertically downwards**.
It is found from $W = m g$ and, being a force, is measured in **newtons**.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Friction acts on an object in the direction in which it is moving.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
Friction is a **resistive** force: it always acts to **oppose** the motion, so it points in the opposite direction to the way the object is moving.
Air resistance behaves the same way, which is why a falling object meets a resistive force acting upwards.

front_blocks.md: An astronaut takes a 12 kg toolbox to the Moon. Which of its mass and its weight changes, and why?

back_blocks.md: Its **mass** does not change.
Mass is a scalar measure of the amount of matter in an object, in kilograms, and it is the same everywhere in the universe.
Its **weight** does change, because weight depends on $g$, the acceleration due to gravity, and $g$ is smaller on the Moon than on Earth.

front_blocks.md: In mechanics, define a **particle**.

back_blocks.md: A **particle** is an object modelled as having **negligible dimensions**, so that it occupies a single point in space.
Because it has no size, **air resistance cannot act on it** and can be left out of the model.

front_blocks.md: A string is modelled as **light**. What does that mean, and what does it let you assume about the tension?

back_blocks.md: **Light** means the string is modelled as having **zero mass**.
There is then no weight anywhere along it to be supported, so the **tension is the same at every point** of the string.

front_blocks.md: Fill in the blanks to complete the two surface assumptions:
A `\_\_\_\_\_\_` surface exerts no frictional force on an object in contact with it, while a `\_\_\_\_\_\_` surface does.

back_blocks.md: The completed statement is:
A **smooth** surface exerts no frictional force on an object in contact with it, while a **rough** surface does.
Modelling a surface as smooth is what allows friction to be left out of the equations altogether.

front_blocks.md: Two particles are joined by an **inextensible** string. What does inextensible mean, and what does it let you assume about the two particles?

back_blocks.md: **Inextensible** means the string cannot be **stretched**, so its length is fixed.
Whatever distance one particle moves, the other must move the same distance, so at every moment the two have the **same speed** and **accelerations of equal magnitude**.

front_blocks.md: A pulley is modelled as **light and smooth**. What does the **smooth** part let you assume about the tension?

back_blocks.md: That the **tension is the same on both sides** of the pulley.
A smooth pulley exerts no friction on the string passing over it, so nothing acts to make the tension on one side differ from the tension on the other.

front_blocks.md: What does it mean to model a rod as **uniform**, and what does that let you assume about its weight?

back_blocks.md: **Uniform** means the rod's mass is distributed **evenly** along its length.
Its whole weight can therefore be taken to act at the **midpoint** of the rod, rather than being spread along it.

front_blocks.md: A rod is modelled as **rigid**. What does that let you assume about it?

back_blocks.md: That it does not **bend** or change shape under the forces acting on it.
Its length stays fixed and the points at which the forces act stay in the same places, which is what makes it possible to work with distances measured along it.
